title: Green's Theorem
body:
Converts a [[Line Integral]] around a closed curve in the plane into a [[Double Integral]] over the
region it encloses.

$$
\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right) dA
$$

with $C$ the boundary of $D$, traversed **counterclockwise** (positive orientation: the region
stays on your left). The integrand on the right is the scalar [[Curl]] of $\mathbf{F} = \langle P,Q\rangle$,
so the statement reads: **total circulation around the boundary equals the curl added up over the
inside.**

## Why it is true, in one sentence

Adjacent tiny loops inside $D$ cancel along their shared edges, because each edge is traversed once
in each direction, so summing circulation over every tiny loop leaves only the outer boundary. Same
telescoping argument as the [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]], and the same reason all three of
this course's big theorems have the shape *integral of a derivative inside = integral of the thing
on the boundary*.

## The flux form

$$
\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\,ds = \iint_D (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F})\,dA
$$

Same theorem with the normal instead of the tangent: circulation form involves [[Curl]], flux form
involves [[Divergence]]. The flux form is the [[Divergence Theorem]] in two dimensions, exactly as
the circulation form is [[Stokes' Theorem]] flattened.

## What it is for

- **Awkward loop integrals**: when parameterising four sides of a rectangle is worse than one
  double integral, swap
- **Area**: taking $Q = x$, $P = 0$ gives $\text{Area}(D) = \oint_C x\,dy$, which is how a
  planimeter works and how a polygon's area gets computed from its vertices in graphics code
- **Detecting a hole**: if $Q_x = P_y$ everywhere but the loop integral is nonzero, the region is
  not simply connected. See the counterexample in [[Conservative Vector Field]]

The hypotheses matter: $C$ must be simple (no self-crossings), closed, positively oriented, and
$P, Q$ must have continuous partials on all of $D$, holes included.

## Related

- [[Stokes' Theorem]]: this is its flat case, and [[Divergence Theorem]] the volume analogue
- [[Curl]] and [[Divergence]]: the two integrands
- [[Line Integral]], [[Double Integral]] in [[CALCULUS 2]]
- [[Conservative Vector Field]]: the zero-curl case, where both sides vanish
- [[Vector Calculus]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]
